lead: Static CMOS waits for inputs; dynamic logic uses a clock to precharge a node high, then evaluate a pull-down network. This saves transistors and can be faster, but the floating dynamic node brings charge sharing and leakage problems. Domino logic adds an inverter so gates can cascade, and cascode voltage switch logic (CVSL) uses a cross-coupled pMOS pair for differential outputs. These styles appear in high-speed datapaths and adders. The cost is clock power, careful timing and extra design rules.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.3 for capacitance and Chapter 3.8 for pass transistors.

blocks.text: A dynamic gate has a clock φ (phi). When φ = 0, a pMOS precharge transistor connects the dynamic node to V<sub>DD</sub>. The node voltage V<sub>dyn</sub> becomes V<sub>DD</sub>. The evaluate nMOS is off, so the pull-down network cannot discharge.

When φ = 1, precharge turns off and evaluate turns on. If the NMOS pull-down network conducts, it discharges C<sub>dyn</sub> to 0 V. If the network is off, the node stays high only because C<sub>dyn</sub> stores charge. It is dynamic: the value is held by capacitance, not by a DC path.

items: Set φ = 0: precharge C<sub>dyn</sub> to V<sub>DD</sub>; the dynamic node is high.
Set φ = 1: evaluate the NMOS pull-down network.
Inputs high enough: C<sub>dyn</sub> discharges to 0 V.
Inputs low: C<sub>dyn</sub> stays high; leakage slowly removes charge.

blocks.text: A dynamic NAND with n inputs uses n series nMOS devices, one evaluate nMOS and one precharge pMOS. Static CMOS needs 2n transistors for the same NAND. The saving is large for wide gates. The clock line drives many transistors, so its power and skew matter.

Charge sharing happens when an internal node with capacitance C<sub>int</sub> connects to C<sub>dyn</sub> during evaluation. The charge on C<sub>dyn</sub> is shared, so V<sub>dyn</sub> falls even if the pull-down path is not complete to ground. If the drop crosses the inverter threshold, the output flips wrongly.

blocks.where: C<sub>dyn</sub> is the dynamic node capacitance in farads (F); C<sub>int</sub> is the internal node capacitance in F; V<sub>pre</sub> is the precharged voltage in volts (V); V<sub>int</sub> is the internal node voltage before connection in V; V<sub>dyn</sub> is the final shared voltage in V.

blocks.text: A keeper transistor is a weak pMOS from V<sub>DD</sub> to the dynamic node. Its gate is driven by the output of the inverter, that is, by the gate output node. When the node should stay high, the keeper supplies leakage current and fights charge sharing. The keeper must be weak enough that the NMOS pull-down can still discharge the node during evaluation.

Charge sharing is reduced by precharging internal nodes, by adding dummy capacitance, or by keeping C<sub>int</sub> small. Leakage sets a minimum clock frequency: if the clock runs too slowly, the dynamic node may droop before evaluation. Dynamic gates therefore suit continuous high-speed operation, not long pauses.

sections.h3: Domino logic and the non-inverting rule

blocks.text: A dynamic gate cannot drive another dynamic gate directly in a simple cascade. During precharge, every dynamic output goes high. The next gate would see a high input and may start evaluating with the wrong value. Domino logic adds an inverter after the dynamic node.

The inverter output is low during precharge. During evaluation it can only rise from 0 to 1, never fall. A chain of domino gates therefore evaluates in order, like falling dominoes. The overall gate is non-inverting: the pull-down condition is inverted at the dynamic node and inverted again at the output.

Because the output makes only low-to-high transitions in evaluation, a domino gate can feed another domino gate safely. Inverting logic inside a domino stage needs differential or special techniques. Domino is common in high-speed adders and critical datapaths, but clock power and charge sharing remain.

Domino logic is grouped with other clocked logic families such as clocked CMOS (C²MOS), NORA and TSPC, but it is not the same circuit. NORA and TSPC are clocked dynamic families: NORA uses alternating clock phases, and TSPC uses a true single-phase clock. Only a few universities teach NORA and TSPC in detail; know their names and purpose.

CVSL is a differential logic family. It has two NMOS pull-down networks: one for the true function and one for its complement. Two cross-coupled pMOS transistors act as the load. The pMOS gate of each side connects to the other output node.

During evaluation, one NMOS network conducts and pulls its output low. The cross-coupled pMOS whose gate is low turns on and holds the other output high. The circuit therefore produces both the true and complement outputs. The NMOS network must be strong enough to overpower the pMOS keeper, so CVSL is ratioed during switching.

CVSL can implement complex functions in one gate because it uses both true and complement inputs. The cost is more wiring, more transistors and careful sizing. It is used in complex high-speed logic where differential signals are available.

items: Static CMOS: complementary networks, no clock, robust, 2n transistors for an n-input gate.
Dynamic: clocked precharge and evaluate; for an n-input NAND, n pull-down nMOS plus one evaluate and one precharge transistor (n+2), before adding a keeper or output inverter.
Domino: dynamic plus inverter, cascadable, non-inverting.
CVSL: differential, cross-coupled pMOS load, ratioed during switching.

figure.caption: The clock is low for precharge and high for evaluate. The output is valid only after evaluation starts, so the next stage must wait.

spec.aria: A clocked timeline: precharge while the clock is low, evaluate while it is high.

examples.question: A dynamic node C<sub>dyn</sub> = 50 fF is precharged to V<sub>pre</sub> = 1.8 V. An internal node C<sub>int</sub> = 10 fF starts at V<sub>int</sub> = 0 V and connects to the dynamic node during evaluation. No keeper is present. Find the final dynamic node voltage.
steps: Before connection, charge on the dynamic node is Q<sub>dyn</sub> = C<sub>dyn</sub>V<sub>pre</sub> = 50 fF × 1.8 V = 90 fC.
Charge on the internal node is Q<sub>int</sub> = C<sub>int</sub>V<sub>int</sub> = 10 fF × 0 V = 0 fC.
After connection, total capacitance is C<sub>total</sub> = C<sub>dyn</sub> + C<sub>int</sub> = 50 fF + 10 fF = 60 fF.
Total charge is conserved: Q<sub>total</sub> = Q<sub>dyn</sub> + Q<sub>int</sub> = 90 fC + 0 fC = 90 fC.
Final voltage is V<sub>dyn</sub> = Q<sub>total</sub> / C<sub>total</sub> = 90 fC / 60 fF = 1.5 V.
examples.answer: The final dynamic node voltage is 1.5 V.
examples.check:
c_dyn = 50e-15
c_int = 10e-15
v_pre = 1.8
v_int = 0.0
q_total = c_dyn * v_pre + c_int * v_int
c_total = c_dyn + c_int
v_final = q_total / c_total
print(v_final)

traps: Cascading dynamic gates without domino inverters; the precharged high output can make the next gate evaluate the wrong value.
Ignoring charge sharing: an internal node at 0 V can pull the dynamic node down even when the pull-down path is off, flipping the output.
Making the keeper too strong: it holds the node high but the NMOS pull-down cannot discharge it, so evaluation fails or slows.
Mixing dynamic and static inputs at different times; inputs must be stable before evaluate and must not glitch.
Calling CVSL non-ratioed: the NMOS network must overpower the cross-coupled pMOS during switching.

quiz.q: What are the two phases of a dynamic gate?
quiz.a: Precharge when the clock is low, and evaluate when the clock is high.

quiz.q: Why does a dynamic gate need a clock?
quiz.a: The clock turns on the precharge pMOS and the evaluate nMOS in turn. The high level is stored on capacitance, so the gate needs a precharge phase before each evaluation.

quiz.q: A dynamic node C<sub>dyn</sub> = 80 fF is precharged to 1.8 V. An internal node C<sub>int</sub> = 20 fF is at 0 V and connects during evaluation. Find the final voltage.
quiz.a: Q = 80 fF × 1.8 V = 144 fC. C<sub>total</sub> = 100 fF. V = 144 fC / 100 fF = 1.44 V.

quiz.q: Why can a domino gate drive another domino gate, while a plain dynamic gate cannot in a simple cascade?
quiz.a: A plain dynamic output is high during precharge, which can falsely turn on the next gate. A domino gate has an inverter, so its output is low during precharge and can only rise during evaluation. This makes the cascade evaluate in order.

quiz.q: What is the role of a keeper transistor?
quiz.a: It is a weak pMOS that holds the dynamic node high against leakage and charge sharing when the pull-down network is off.

quiz.q: CVSL is called ratioed during switching. Explain why.
quiz.a: The conducting NMOS network pulls one output low while a cross-coupled pMOS tries to hold it high. The NMOS must be strong enough to overpower the pMOS, so transistor sizing ratios matter.

quiz.q: A dynamic node C<sub>dyn</sub> = 60 fF is precharged to 1.8 V. An internal node C<sub>int</sub> = 15 fF is at 0.9 V and connects during evaluation. Find the final voltage.

beyond: Not for the exam. Domino logic appears in high-performance processor datapaths, where clock-delayed domino and dual-rail domino help manage timing. CVSL and other differential styles connect to low-swing and high-speed signaling research. Modern finFET and low-voltage designs make charge sharing and keeper sizing more critical. Search for clock-delayed domino, true single-phase clock logic, and differential cascode voltage switch logic to go further.
